Bakers put the rolls in the oven in pairs, so two rolls touch and bake together. Later they break them apart. On your half you get butter, a thick slice of Gouda, strong mustard and rings of raw onion. Gouda is a yellow cheese from the Netherlands. It is soft and a little salty.

blk_part_01_funny_food_names_in_cologne.text: So why the funny name? Nobody knows for sure, and people in Cologne tell different stories. The best-known story takes place at a birthday party in the late 1800s. As a joke, a man ordered half a rooster for each of his friends. He told the waiter his plan first. The friends waited for roast chicken, but the waiter brought rye rolls with cheese. Everyone laughed, and the joke became the name of the dish. It is a nice story, but nobody can say if it is true.

blk_part_01_funny_food_names_in_cologne.text: The second funny name in Cologne is Himmel un Ääd, dialect for heaven and earth. It is mashed potatoes mixed with cooked apples. So it is soft, a little sweet and a little sour. With it you usually get fried black pudding, a dark sausage made with pig's blood. You also get fried onions. The name comes from where the food grows. Apples grow high up in trees, near the sky. In German, Himmel is the word for both sky and heaven. Potatoes grow in the ground, in the earth. So one plate holds heaven and earth.

blk_part_03_mustard_in_d_sseldorf.text: Mustard has been made in Düsseldorf since 1726. In that year, the first mustard factory in Germany opened in the city. The brand ABB says its story starts with that factory. Since 2012, Düsseldorfer Mostert has been a protected name in the European Union. Only mustard made in Düsseldorf may use this name. A company in another city can make mustard in the same way. But it cannot call it Düsseldorfer Mostert. Kölsch has a protected name too. In both cases, the name tells you where the product really comes from.

blk_part_04_a_pepper_stew_in_dortmund.text: Pfefferpotthast is a beef stew: meat cooked slowly in liquid until it is very soft. It is an old dish of Westphalia, the region around Dortmund. It was a meal for working people. The cook fries pieces of beef. Then the beef boils slowly in a pot for a long time, with lots of onions. Bay leaves and plenty of black pepper go in too. The onions almost melt and make the stew sweet, and the pepper makes it spicy.

You eat them hot, with apple sauce. In the Rhineland, people also eat them with Rübenkraut, the sugar-beet syrup from the Sauerbraten part. Hot, salty potato with something sweet is a popular mix here.
